items: Linux (Debian/Ubuntu): sudo apt install git. On Fedora: sudo dnf install git.
macOS: install the Xcode Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install) or use Homebrew: brew install git for a newer version.
Windows: install Git for Windows, which includes Git Bash, a credential manager and optional integration with the Windows terminal.
CI runners: GitHub-hosted runners already ship with a recent Git version.

blocks.text: Git reads configuration from several files. More specific levels override broader ones, so a repository can use a different email than your global default.

rows: /etc/gitconfig (Git for Windows: inside the install directory)
Every repository of the current user

blocks.text: Precedence, from strongest to weakest: worktree, local, global, system. The last value read wins, and Git reads the most specific file last. Command-line overrides such as git -c key=value beat all of them.

$ git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
$ git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
$ git config --global init.defaultBranch main
$ git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
$ git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3
$ git config --global fetch.prune true

# Inspect everything, and see which file each value came from
$ git config --list --show-origin
$ git config --show-origin user.email
file:/home/ada/.gitconfig    ada@example.com

items: user.name and user.email are written into every commit you create. GitHub uses the email to link commits to your account.
init.defaultBranch sets the name of the first branch in new repositories.
core.editor is used for commit messages, interactive rebase and more. The --wait flag makes Git wait until you close the file in a GUI editor.
merge.conflictStyle zdiff3 also shows the common ancestor inside conflict markers, which makes conflicts much easier to resolve (Module 2).
fetch.prune removes remote-tracking branches that were deleted on the server.

blocks.text: Windows uses CRLF line endings; Linux and macOS use LF. Without a policy, a Windows and a Mac developer can produce diffs where every line appears changed. Git can normalize this in two ways.

rows: Convert LF to CRLF on checkout, CRLF to LF on commit
Convert CRLF to LF on commit only

blocks.text: A per-user setting cannot enforce consistency across a team. The robust solution is a committed .gitattributes file, which applies to everyone who clones the repository:

blocks.code:
# Normalize all text files to LF in the repository
* text=auto eol=lf

# Windows scripts must keep CRLF
*.bat text eol=crlf
*.ps1 text eol=crlf

# Never touch binary files
*.png binary
*.jpg binary
*.zip binary

blocks.text: Different Identities for Work and Personal Projects
Conditional includes let Git load extra configuration based on where a repository lives. This is the standard way to avoid committing to your employer's repositories with your personal email.

blocks.code:
# ~/.gitconfig
[user]
    name = Ada Lovelace
    email = ada@personal.dev

[includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"]
    path = ~/.gitconfig-work

# ~/.gitconfig-work
[user]
    email = ada.lovelace@company.com

[alias]
    st = status -sb
    co = checkout
    sw = switch
    lg = log --oneline --graph --decorate --all
    last = log -1 HEAD --stat
    unstage = restore --staged

blocks.text: If you do not want your real email to be public, GitHub provides a noreply address (ID+username@users.noreply.github.com) under Settings > Emails. Commits made with it are still attributed to your account.
